extracted.intended_audience: junior mathematicians (early-career researchers) making choices about what to publish
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for early-career mathematicians on which results to write up and publish, and how to judge others' papers — with emphasis on building a coherent research narrative versus inflating paper counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit into a coherent research narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: If your little paper fits the narrative, do write it and publish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work you publish should help you tell a good colloquium-style story about your work. A good talk requires coherence — background, major open problems, how your sequence of work positions you for the recent advance. Avoid a patchwork quilt of disparate one-off results; prefer results that connect to a main line of research or form a series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve a major open problem
rubrics_metrics.description: You can solve a major open problem — the talk writes itself then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theorem of major significance stands alone: state the background, sketch the proof idea, and the result speaks for itself. No follow-up or strong narrative is needed in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a series / recognizable style
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing as a 'series' or developing a recognizable style is valuable (analogy to Monet's haystacks, Van Gogh's sunflowers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series are valued because they show sustained development and identity; having multiple coherent papers that build technology and culminate in an advance is preferable to many unrelated one-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small nice results plus exceptional exposition/lecturing
rubrics_metrics.description: You can prove something small and nice, but be an amazing lecturer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can present minor results in a way that captivates an audience, the work can still have positive career impact (e.g., securing a job via an excellent talk). Exceptional communication can amplify the value of modest technical contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid one-off papers that distract from your main story
rubrics_metrics.description: If it’s a one-off thing that distracts from your main line of research — why tell anyone?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-off publications that do not fit your narrative are likely to dilute your CV and may harm job prospects; keep peripheral results private until they can be positioned within a coherent program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge papers by validity and relative importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the paper, make a judgement on the validity and relative importance of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assess correctness and significance first. Supplement that assessment with knowledge about the authors and how the community has received their previous work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement reading with author reputation and prior reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement the judgement with what you know about the author, just like when you judge a painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at how previous papers by the author were accepted by the community (citations, retractions, reception). Prior record can inform whether a new paper is likely to be valuable or part of a pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for problematic patterns: many repeated coauthors / cliques
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a clique: build a group of 5-8 close collaborators, write many papers in different subsets, cite heavily within the clique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such patterns inflate publication counts without necessarily increasing independent contribution. As an editor/referee, check for repeated names and heavy mutual citation; avoid referees from the same clique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of cartel-like behavior and manufactured fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a cartel: invent an area, apply for collaborative grants, organize conferences, publish proceedings, start journals — create appearances of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quantitative strategy can look legitimate externally but can be used to game metrics. Treat manufactured clusters with skepticism; evaluate the intrinsic merit rather than apparent community infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about publishing in little-known, low-selectivity, or shady journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish in little known, not very selective or shady journals (example: many papers in an MDPI journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing heavily in such journals can inflate numbers but may not signal genuine impact; check journal indexing (e.g., MathSciNet) and editorial practices. While not always formally unethical, these choices can harm long-term reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for editors publishing many papers in their own journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Become an editor of a not well managed journal and publish a lot there with all your collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial control can be abused to publish large numbers of papers from the same group. This is a red flag; factor editorial role and journal oversight into your assessment of the work's merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect zero-knowledge publishing / coordinated, misleading publication strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Zero-knowledge publishing: produce many papers that give the vibe of progress on A=?Z without actually proving the target; combine two lists of equivalent statements so a later accepted paper can be used to claim a final result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for multiple parallel papers proving different reductions, many with missing details or minor errors, differing coauthor patterns (famous coauthors on some, many grad students on others). If you see many parallel 'steps' and a history of fragile or dropped papers, suspect coordinated gaming and treat claims cautiously; do not accept until a definitive, clear, correct paper appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for retractions, known mistakes, or repeated abandoned papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Have any of their papers been retracted or major mistakes found? Do they have several parallel papers which prove not exactly related results towards the same goal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A history of retractions, persistent mistakes, or many abandoned attempts toward the same claim undermines credibility. Use such history to downgrade trust in new claims until corrected or a definitive proof is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate discoverability and prior literature coverage (self-citation issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author has many similar short papers with mostly self-citations, it may be hard to check whether the work was done before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For short combinatorial/identity-type results, ensure that the literature review and indexing make the contribution discoverable; heavy self-citation and poor linkage to existing literature decrease usefulness and may justify rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When hiring/postdoc selection, match candidate profile to institutional needs
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a postdoc to work closely and build something, hire someone with fewer but coherent papers; if you want adaptability and many collaborations, prefer the candidate with many diverse papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you need a broadly productive independent researcher or someone who will integrate into a focused program. Consider how much supervision is available and how well the candidate's publication pattern predicts future behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers (paper counts, h-index, citations) are imperfect and manipulable
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of papers is what’s causing you to worry... numbers rule the world but can be inflated by social strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metrics as noisy signals. Understand mechanisms that inflate metrics (cliques, cartels, editorial practices, non-indexed journals) and prefer qualitative judgment of significance and coherence over raw counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of special issues and guest-editor roles used to inflate output
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize special issues with journals to publish many related papers (example: 11 special issues served as special editor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special-issue activity can be legitimate but also used to facilitate publication of many papers from a group. Check editorial oversight and peer-review standards for such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind reviews may be less useful in math contexts (author opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: I realize that many well meaning journals have double blind reviews. I understand where they are coming from, but think in the case of math this is misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author expresses skepticism; implication for practice: in math, knowledge of author and their record can be informative when assessing submissions. (Note: this is an opinionated guideline rather than a formal rule.)
